We need to propose a retrosynthesis route up to 3 steps, leaves must be commercially available chemicals, total price <= $9999. Need to output JSON tree with reactions and template IDs.

We have many templates from search. Need to pick plausible disconnections.

Target: Cc1ccc(NS(=O)(=O)c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2)cc1

Structure: a tolyl sulfonamide attached to a phenyl ring bearing a trans-α,β-unsaturated amide (anilide) with an aniline at the amide nitrogen (anilide). So overall: p-tolyl-sulfonyl-phenyl-CH=CH-CO-NH-phenyl-NH2? Actually the amide nitrogen is attached to an aniline (c3ccccc3N). So it's a phenylcarboxamide with an aniline substituent (anilide). So we can disconnect at sulfonamide formation (sulfonyl chloride + aniline). Also disconnect at amide formation (acid chloride + aniline). Also disconnect at the C=C double bond (maybe via Wittig or Heck). Simpler: two steps: 1) Form sulfonamide from p-tolyl sulfonyl chloride and 4-aminophenyl-... Actually the sulfonyl chloride would be p-tolylsulfonyl chloride (p-CH3C6H4SO2Cl). React with aniline of the other phenyl (the phenyl bearing the side chain). That gives sulfonamide.

Second step: form the amide via coupling of 4-aminophenyl (aniline) with trans-cinnamic acid derivative? Actually we need the side chain: phenyl-CH=CH-CO-NH-Ph-NH2. Could be formed by coupling aniline (c3ccccc3N) with trans-cinnamic acid (c2ccc(/C=C/COOH)cc2) via amide formation (using coupling reagent). But we also need the double bond; could start from trans-cinnamic acid (commercial) and couple with aniline to give trans-cinnamamide (Ph-CH=CH-CO-NH-Ph). Then we need an extra NH2 on the phenyl (the aniline). Actually the amide nitrogen is attached to phenyl with NH2 substituent (aniline). So trans-cinnamoyl chloride + 4-aminophenyl (p-aminophenyl) gives the amide with NH2 para to the amide? Wait the SMILES: /C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N. That is trans-CH=CH-CO-NH-Ph-NH2 (aniline attached at para? Actually the phenyl is unsubstituted except the NH2 at position 1 (attached to carbonyl). So it's an anilide where the amide nitrogen is attached to phenyl that also has an NH2 at para? No, the SMILES: Nc3ccccc3N means an aniline with an NH attached to carbonyl (N attached to carbonyl) and also an NH2 on the phenyl? Actually "Nc3ccccc3N" means N attached to carbonyl (the amide N) is attached to aromatic carbon (c3) which also has an N substituent (the terminal N). So the phenyl has an NH2 at the other position (maybe ortho). So the phenyl is an aniline (NH2) and also attached via its carbon to the amide nitrogen. So it's 2-aminophenyl amide? The SMILES: Nc3ccccc3N: the first N is the amide N attached to aromatic carbon; the second N is an exocyclic NH2 on the aromatic ring. So it's 2-aminobenzamide? Actually the amide N attaches to the aromatic carbon at position 1, and the aromatic also has an NH2 at position 1? That seems ambiguous. But we can treat as an aniline with an amide attached to the ring (like anthranilamide). So we need a 2-aminobenzamide derivative.

Thus we could start from 2-aminobenzoyl chloride (or 2-aminobenzoic acid) and do a Heck coupling to introduce the C=C? Actually the double bond is conjugated to carbonyl, typical cinnamamide. Could be formed via Knoevenagel condensation of benzaldehyde with malonic acid then amidation. Simpler: use commercially available trans-cinnamoyl chloride (or trans-cinnamic acid) and couple with 2-aminophenylamine? Wait we need both amide N and NH2 on same phenyl. So we need 2-aminobenzylamine? Actually the amide nitrogen is attached to the phenyl carbon, not to the NH2. So the phenyl has an NH2 substituent (para? maybe ortho). So we need 2-aminobenzylamine? Not.

Better approach: Use commercially available 2-aminobenzaldehyde (or 2-aminobenzylamine) to build the cinnamamide via Wittig? Might be too many steps.

Given limit 3 steps, we can propose:

Step 1: Sulfonamide formation: p-toluenesulfonyl chloride + 4-(2-aminophenyl)-cinnamamide (the rest of molecule) -> target.

Step 2: Amide formation: trans-cinnamic acid + 2-aminobenzenamine? Actually we need amide where nitrogen attached to phenyl (which also has NH2). So we can use 2-aminobenzylamine? Wait the amide nitrogen is attached to phenyl carbon (C=O-N-Ph). So the amide nitrogen is part of the side chain, not the NH2 on phenyl. So we need an aniline (2-aminophenyl) as nucleophile to react with trans-cinnamoyl chloride, giving trans-cinnamamide with an ortho NH2 substituent on the phenyl. That product is trans-cinnamoyl-2-aminophenyl amide (i.e., 2-aminobenzamide of cinnamic acid). That matches the SMILES: /C=C/C(=O)N-Ph-NH2 (where the N attached to carbonyl is attached to phenyl at position 1, and the phenyl has an NH2 at position 2). So step 2: trans-cinnamoyl chloride + 2-aminophenyl (o-aminophenyl) -> amide.

Thus we need trans-cinnamoyl chloride (commercial) and o-aminophenyl (2-aminophenyl) maybe as 2-aminophenylamine? Actually we need the amine (2-aminophenyl) as nucleophile. That's 2-aminophenyl (aniline). Commercially available 2-aminophenyl (2-aminophenyl) is 2-aminophenyl (o-aminophenyl) i.e., o-phenylenediamine? Wait o-phenylenediamine is 1,2-diaminobenzene (two NH2). Our required is only one NH2 on phenyl (the other position is attached to amide). So we need 2-aminobenzylamine? No, we need 2-aminophenyl (aniline) which is 2-aminobenzene (o-aminophenyl). That's o-aminophenyl (C6H6N). That's o-aminobenzene (C6H7N). That's commercially available (o-phenylenediamine has two NH2). But we need only one NH2; we can use o-aminophenyl (2-aminophenyl) which is same as aniline with NH2 at ortho position? Actually aniline is C6H5NH2; the NH2 is attached to the ring. The position is not defined; it's just aniline. For ortho substitution, we need a substituent at ortho relative to the amide attachment, but the amide attaches at the same carbon as the NH2? Wait the amide attaches to the aromatic carbon, not to the NH2. So the phenyl has two substituents: the amide nitrogen attached to carbon (C=O-N-Ph) and an NH2 substituent on the ring. So the phenyl is 2-aminophenyl (i.e., aniline with an extra substituent at ortho). The amide attaches at position 1, NH2 at position 2. So the nucleophile is 2-aminophenylamine? Actually the amide nitrogen is the nucleophile; the aromatic carbon is part of the ring, not a nucleophile. So we need 2-aminophenylamine? No, we need 2-aminophenyl (the aromatic ring) as part of the amide product; the amide nitrogen is external (coming from the acid chloride). So we need 2-aminophenylamine? Wait the amide nitrogen is attached to carbonyl and to aromatic carbon (forming anilide). So the amide nitrogen is part of the product, not a starting material. Starting materials: trans-cinnamoyl chloride (or acid) and 2-aminophenylamine? Actually to form an amide, you need an amine and an acid chloride. The amine is the nucleophile. Here the amine is the 2-aminophenyl (aniline) which has an NH2 group that will become the amide nitrogen? But the amide nitrogen is attached to the aromatic carbon, not the NH2. In anilide formation, the amine is aniline (C6H5NH2) reacting with acid chloride gives C6H5-NH-CO-... So the amine's nitrogen becomes the amide nitrogen. So we need aniline (with NH2) as nucleophile. The product will have the amide nitrogen attached to the phenyl (the same phenyl). The phenyl also has an NH2 substituent elsewhere (maybe at ortho). That means the starting aniline must be 2-aminophenyl (i.e., 2-aminobenzenamine) which has two NH2 groups: one will react to form amide, the other remains as NH2. That's o-phenylenediamine (1,2-diaminobenzene). Yes! So starting material: o-phenylenediamine (C6H4(NH2)2). React one NH2 with trans-cinnamoyl chloride to give the desired amide with remaining NH2 intact. Good.

Thus step 2: o-phenylenediamine + trans-cinnamoyl chloride -> trans-cinnamoyl-2-aminophenyl amide (product B). This is a standard acylation.

Step 1: sulfonamide formation: p-toluenesulfonyl chloride + product B (which has an aniline? Actually product B has a free NH2 on the phenyl (the second NH2). But sulfonamide attaches to a different phenyl (p-tolyl) via sulfonyl group attached to the other phenyl (the one with methyl). Wait the sulfonamide in target is attached to the p-tolyl ring (the sulfonyl group attached to p-tolyl) and the sulfonamide nitrogen attached to the other phenyl (the phenyl bearing the cinnamamide). So the sulfonamide nitrogen is the same as the amide nitrogen? No, the sulfonamide nitrogen is the same as the nitrogen attached to the sulfonyl group and to the phenyl bearing the side chain. In target: Cc1ccc(NS(=O)(=O)c2ccc(... )cc2)cc1. So the sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to the p-tolyl ring (as substituent) and to the other phenyl (c2...). So the nitrogen is bridging between two aromatic rings via sulfonyl group. So the sulfonamide nitrogen is part of the sulfonamide, not the amide. The amide nitrogen is separate (attached to carbonyl). So the sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to the phenyl bearing the cinnamamide side chain. That phenyl currently has the amide substituent at para? Actually the phenyl (c2ccc(... )cc2) has the side chain at para relative to the sulfonamide attachment? The SMILES: c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2 attached to sulfonyl via S(=O)(=O)N. So the sulfonamide nitrogen attaches to that phenyl at position 1, and the side chain is at para (position 4). So that phenyl has two substituents: sulfonamide N and the cinnamamide side chain.

Thus product B (from step 2) is the phenyl with amide side chain and an NH2 (the other amine). But we need the sulfonamide nitrogen attached to that phenyl, not the NH2. So we need to convert the remaining NH2 on product B into sulfonamide with p-toluenesulfonyl chloride, forming N-sulfonylation. That gives target.

Thus overall 2 steps: 1) acylation of o-phenylenediamine with trans-cinnamoyl chloride -> intermediate A (2-aminophenyl cinnamamide). 2) sulfonylation of the remaining NH2 with p-toluenesulfonyl chloride -> target.

That's 2 steps, within limit.

Now need to find templates for amide formation (acyl chloride + amine) and sulfonylation (sulfonyl chloride + amine). Use search to find templates IDs.

Search for amide formation: product target? Let's search for template that forms amide from acid chloride and amine. Use functional_groups_formed ["amides"] but earlier error because "amides" not valid; correct is "amide". Let's search with "amide".
